claim: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) are a class of devastating neurological disorders characterized by recurrent seizures and exacerbated by disruptions to excitatory/inhibitory balance in the brain.
source: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs), a class of devastating neurological disorders characterized by recurrent seizures and exacerbated by disruptions to excitatory/inhibitory balance in the brain, are commonly caused by mutations in ion channels.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about DEEs presented in the abstract as established knowledge in the field.

claim: DEEs are commonly caused by mutations in ion channels.
source: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs), a class of devastating neurological disorders characterized by recurrent seizures and exacerbated by disruptions to excitatory/inhibitory balance in the brain, are commonly caused by mutations in ion channels.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge about the genetic causes of DEEs.

claim: Disruption of, or variants in, FGF13 were implicated as causal for a set of DEEs.
source: Disruption of, or variants in, FGF13 were implicated as causal for a set of DEEs, but the underlying mechanisms were clouded because FGF13 is expressed in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons, FGF13 undergoes extensive alternative splicing producing multiple isoforms with distinct functions, and the overall roles of FGF13 in neurons are incompletely cataloged.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing the link between FGF13 and DEEs.

claim: FGF13 is expressed in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
source: Disruption of, or variants in, FGF13 were implicated as causal for a set of DEEs, but the underlying mechanisms were clouded because FGF13 is expressed in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons, FGF13 undergoes extensive alternative splicing producing multiple isoforms with distinct functions, and the overall roles of FGF13 in neurons are incompletely cataloged.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge and is supported by citations in the manuscript (Puranam et al., 2015; Joglekar et al., 2021).

claim: FGF13 undergoes extensive alternative splicing producing multiple isoforms with distinct functions.
source: Disruption of, or variants in, FGF13 were implicated as causal for a set of DEEs, but the underlying mechanisms were clouded because FGF13 is expressed in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons, FGF13 undergoes extensive alternative splicing producing multiple isoforms with distinct functions, and the overall roles of FGF13 in neurons are incompletely cataloged.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior literature on FGF13 alternative splicing (Munoz-Sanjuan et al., 2000; Puranam et al., 2015).

claim: Interneuron-targeted deletion of Fgf13 led to perinatal mortality associated with extensive seizures.
source: Interneuron-targeted deletion of Fgf13 led to perinatal mortality associated with extensive seizures and impaired the hippocampal inhibitory/excitatory balance while excitatory neuron-targeted deletion of Fgf13 caused no detectable seizures and no survival deficits.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from the Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice.

claim: Interneuron-targeted deletion of Fgf13 impaired the hippocampal inhibitory/excitatory balance.
source: Interneuron-targeted deletion of Fgf13 led to perinatal mortality associated with extensive seizures and impaired the hippocampal inhibitory/excitatory balance while excitatory neuron-targeted deletion of Fgf13 caused no detectable seizures and no survival deficits.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data showing increased sEPSC frequency and decreased sIPSC frequency in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice.

claim: Excitatory neuron-targeted deletion of Fgf13 caused no detectable seizures and no survival deficits.
source: Interneuron-targeted deletion of Fgf13 led to perinatal mortality associated with extensive seizures and impaired the hippocampal inhibitory/excitatory balance while excitatory neuron-targeted deletion of Fgf13 caused no detectable seizures and no survival deficits.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Emx1-Fgf13 cKO mice showing normal survival and no seizures.

claim: Fgf13 ablation in interneurons had no effect on voltage-gated sodium channels (Navs).
source: While best studied as a voltage-gated sodium channel (Nav) regulator, we observed no effect of Fgf13 ablation in interneurons on Navs but rather a marked reduction in K+ channel currents.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing no differences in Na+ current properties in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO interneurons.

claim: Fgf13 ablation in interneurons resulted in a marked reduction in K+ channel currents.
source: While best studied as a voltage-gated sodium channel (Nav) regulator, we observed no effect of Fgf13 ablation in interneurons on Navs but rather a marked reduction in K+ channel currents.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data showing reduced K+ current density in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO interneurons.

claim: Re-expressing different Fgf13 splice isoforms could partially rescue deficits in interneuron excitability.
source: Re-expressing different Fgf13 splice isoforms could partially rescue deficits in interneuron excitability and restore K+ channel current amplitude.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments showing that viral re-expression of Fgf13-VY or Fgf13-S partially restored action potential firing.

claim: Re-expressing different Fgf13 splice isoforms could restore K+ channel current amplitude.
source: Re-expressing different Fgf13 splice isoforms could partially rescue deficits in interneuron excitability and restore K+ channel current amplitude.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that Fgf13-S re-expression increased K+ current density to WT levels.

claim: DEEs affect 4 in 10,000 infants per year.
source: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies are a devastating group of rare epilepsies and neurodevelopmental disorders (Scheffer et al., 2016; Scheffer et al., 2017; Scheffer and Liao, 2020) that affect 4 in 10,000 infants per year (Covanis, 2012; Ware et al., 2019).
evidence: This epidemiological statistic is supported by citations to prior literature (Covanis, 2012; Ware et al., 2019).

claim: DEEs are characterized by repeated seizures and severe developmental delay.
source: DEEs are characterized by repeated seizures, severe developmental delay, and are often drug resistant.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about DEEs based on established clinical knowledge.

claim: DEEs are often drug resistant.
source: DEEs are characterized by repeated seizures, severe developmental delay, and are often drug resistant.
evidence: This is a clinical characteristic of DEEs based on established knowledge.

claim: Febrile seizures can contribute to the progression of DEE disease.
source: Febrile seizures, which are more common in young children, can contribute to the progression of disease (Skotte et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Skotte et al., 2022).

claim: DEEs are lethal when the seizures lead to sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP).
source: DEEs are lethal when the seizures lead to sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP; Scheffer and Nabbout, 2019; Chilcott et al., 2022; Donnan et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature on SUDEP (Scheffer and Nabbout, 2019; Chilcott et al., 2022; Donnan et al., 2023).

claim: Variants in ion channels and their auxiliary proteins are among the best-characterized genetic causes for DEEs.
source: Although not all DEEs have been linked to a genetic basis, variants in ion channels and their auxiliary proteins are among the best-characterized genetic causes for DEEs, and sodium channelopathies have been identified as a top cause (Meisler et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature (Meisler et al., 2021).

claim: Sodium channelopathies have been identified as a top cause of DEEs.
source: Although not all DEEs have been linked to a genetic basis, variants in ion channels and their auxiliary proteins are among the best-characterized genetic causes for DEEs, and sodium channelopathies have been identified as a top cause (Meisler et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Meisler et al., 2021).

claim: Epilepsy-associated variants in voltage-gated sodium channels exert gain-of-function effects in excitatory neurons or loss-of-function effects in inhibitory neurons, leading to an overall pro-excitatory state.
source: Epilepsy-associated variants in voltage-gated sodium channels, necessary for action potential initiation, exert gain-of-function effects in excitatory neurons or loss-of-function effects in inhibitory neurons, leading to an overall pro-excitatory state.
evidence: This is a mechanistic statement supported by established knowledge and citations in the field.

claim: Gain-of-function variants in SCN8A coding for NaV1.6 affect excitatory neurons of the forebrain and lead to network hyperexcitability that drives seizures.
source: Gain-of-function variants in SCN8A coding for the neuronal sodium channel NaV1.6 (Adam et al., 1993; Bunton-Stasyshyn et al., 2019; Meisler, 2019; Talwar and Hammer, 2021) or SCN2A coding for NaV1.2 (Kim et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021Miao et al., 2020) affect excitatory neurons of the forebrain, and lead to network hyperexcitability that drives seizures.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature (Adam et al., 1993; Bunton-Stasyshyn et al., 2019; Meisler, 2019; Talwar and Hammer, 2021).

claim: Gain-of-function variants in SCN2A coding for NaV1.2 affect excitatory neurons of the forebrain and lead to network hyperexcitability that drives seizures.
source: Gain-of-function variants in SCN8A coding for the neuronal sodium channel NaV1.6 (Adam et al., 1993; Bunton-Stasyshyn et al., 2019; Meisler, 2019; Talwar and Hammer, 2021) or SCN2A coding for NaV1.2 (Kim et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021Miao et al., 2020) affect excitatory neurons of the forebrain, and lead to network hyperexcitability that drives seizures.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature (Kim et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021; Miao et al., 2020).

claim: Loss-of-function variants in SCN1A coding for NaV1.1 reduce inhibitory drive to excitatory neurons and drive network hyperexcitability as the mechanism for seizures.
source: In contrast, loss-of-function variants in SCN1A coding for NaV1.1, the most abundant NaV expressed in forebrain inhibitory neurons, reduce inhibitory drive to excitatory neurons and thus drive network hyperexcitability as the mechanism for seizures (Vormstein-Schneider et al., 2020; Ding et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Vormstein-Schneider et al., 2020; Ding et al., 2021).

claim: NaV1.1 is the most abundant NaV expressed in forebrain inhibitory neurons.
source: In contrast, loss-of-function variants in SCN1A coding for NaV1.1, the most abundant NaV expressed in forebrain inhibitory neurons, reduce inhibitory drive to excitatory neurons and thus drive network hyperexcitability as the mechanism for seizures (Vormstein-Schneider et al., 2020; Ding et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about NaV1.1 expression.

claim: Variants in NaV1.1 underlie the most common genetic subgroup in Dravet Syndrome.
source: Variants in NaV1.1 underlie the most common genetic subgroup in the prototypical DEE, Dravet Syndrome (Scheffer and Nabbout, 2019; Han et al., 2020, Brunklaus et al., 2022; He et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature (Scheffer and Nabbout, 2019; Han et al., 2020, Brunklaus et al., 2022; He et al., 2022).

claim: DEEs result from variants in NaV auxiliary subunits such as SCN1B.
source: DEEs also result from variants in NaV auxiliary subunits, such as in the NaV beta subunit SCN1B (Patino et al., 2009; Ogiwara et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2013; Ramadan et al., 2017; Bouza and Isom, 2018; Hull et al., 2020) as well as FGF12 (Siekierska et al., 2016; Oda et al., 2019; Saleem et al., 2024) and FGF13 (Puranam et al., 2015; Fry et al., 2021, Velíšková et al., 2021; Narayanan et al., 2022), both fibroblast growth factor homologous factors (FHFs; Goldfarb, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature (Patino et al., 2009; Ogiwara et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2013; Ramadan et al., 2017; Bouza and Isom, 2018; Hull et al., 2020).

claim: DEEs result from variants in FGF12.
source: DEEs also result from variants in NaV auxiliary subunits, such as in the NaV beta subunit SCN1B (Patino et al., 2009; Ogiwara et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2013; Ramadan et al., 2017; Bouza and Isom, 2018; Hull et al., 2020) as well as FGF12 (Siekierska et al., 2016; Oda et al., 2019; Saleem et al., 2024) and FGF13 (Puranam et al., 2015; Fry et al., 2021, Velíšková et al., 2021; Narayanan et al., 2022), both fibroblast growth factor homologous factors (FHFs; Goldfarb, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature (Siekierska et al., 2016; Oda et al., 2019; Saleem et al., 2024).

claim: DEEs result from variants in FGF13.
source: DEEs also result from variants in NaV auxiliary subunits, such as in the NaV beta subunit SCN1B (Patino et al., 2009; Ogiwara et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2013; Ramadan et al., 2017; Bouza and Isom, 2018; Hull et al., 2020) as well as FGF12 (Siekierska et al., 2016; Oda et al., 2019; Saleem et al., 2024) and FGF13 (Puranam et al., 2015; Fry et al., 2021, Velíšková et al., 2021; Narayanan et al., 2022), both fibroblast growth factor homologous factors (FHFs; Goldfarb, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature (Puranam et al., 2015; Fry et al., 2021, Velíšková et al., 2021; Narayanan et al., 2022).

claim: FGF12 and FGF13 are fibroblast growth factor homologous factors (FHFs).
source: DEEs also result from variants in NaV auxiliary subunits, such as in the NaV beta subunit SCN1B (Patino et al., 2009; Ogiwara et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2013; Ramadan et al., 2017; Bouza and Isom, 2018; Hull et al., 2020) as well as FGF12 (Siekierska et al., 2016; Oda et al., 2019; Saleem et al., 2024) and FGF13 (Puranam et al., 2015; Fry et al., 2021, Velíšková et al., 2021; Narayanan et al., 2022), both fibroblast growth factor homologous factors (FHFs; Goldfarb, 2005).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by a citation (Goldfarb, 2005).

claim: FGF13 is a non-canonical fibroblast growth factor that is not secreted and does not bind to FGF receptors.
source: Like other members of the FHF family (FGF11-14), FGF13 is a non-canonical fibroblast growth factor that is not secreted and does not bind to FGF receptors (Schoorlemmer and Goldfarb, 2001; Olsen et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Schoorlemmer and Goldfarb, 2001; Olsen et al., 2003).

claim: FHFs reside in the cytoplasm where they can bind to the intracellular C-terminus of various NaVs and modulate their function.
source: FHFs reside in the cytoplasm where they can bind to the intracellular C-terminus of various NaVs and modulate their function (Goldfarb, 2005; Pablo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Goldfarb, 2005; Pablo et al., 2016).

claim: FGF13 has been shown to be upregulated in the hippocampus of a temporal lobe epilepsy mouse model.
source: FGF13 has been shown to be upregulated in the hippocampus of a temporal lobe epilepsy mouse model, whereas knockdown of Fgf13 attenuated hyperexcitability in hippocampal cells (Shen et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Shen et al., 2022).

claim: Knockdown of Fgf13 attenuated hyperexcitability in hippocampal cells.
source: FGF13 has been shown to be upregulated in the hippocampus of a temporal lobe epilepsy mouse model, whereas knockdown of Fgf13 attenuated hyperexcitability in hippocampal cells (Shen et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Shen et al., 2022).

claim: FGF13 regulates microtubules.
source: Other FGF13 functions, such as the regulation of microtubules (Wu et al., 2012), control of mitogen-activated protein kinases (Lu et al., 2015), and effects on neurodevelopment (Nishimoto and Nishida, 2007) including development of chandelier cells (Favuzzi et al., 2019) have been ascribed, but less well characterized.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Wu et al., 2012).

claim: FGF13 controls mitogen-activated protein kinases.
source: Other FGF13 functions, such as the regulation of microtubules (Wu et al., 2012), control of mitogen-activated protein kinases (Lu et al., 2015), and effects on neurodevelopment (Nishimoto and Nishida, 2007) including development of chandelier cells (Favuzzi et al., 2019) have been ascribed, but less well characterized.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Lu et al., 2015).

claim: FGF13 has effects on neurodevelopment.
source: Other FGF13 functions, such as the regulation of microtubules (Wu et al., 2012), control of mitogen-activated protein kinases (Lu et al., 2015), and effects on neurodevelopment (Nishimoto and Nishida, 2007) including development of chandelier cells (Favuzzi et al., 2019) have been ascribed, but less well characterized.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Nishimoto and Nishida, 2007; Favuzzi et al., 2019).

claim: FGF13 affects development of chandelier cells.
source: Other FGF13 functions, such as the regulation of microtubules (Wu et al., 2012), control of mitogen-activated protein kinases (Lu et al., 2015), and effects on neurodevelopment (Nishimoto and Nishida, 2007) including development of chandelier cells (Favuzzi et al., 2019) have been ascribed, but less well characterized.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Favuzzi et al., 2019).

claim: DEE associated variants in FGF13 are thought to affect NaV function.
source: While DEE associated variants in FGF13 are thought to affect NaV function, this has not been demonstrated in neurons and the contribution of other FGF13 functions has not been investigated, thus preventing an understanding of disease pathology and the development of precision therapies.
evidence: This is a statement about the prevailing hypothesis in the field, which the authors then challenge.

claim: The mechanism by which DEE associated variants in FGF13 affect NaV function has not been demonstrated in neurons.
source: While DEE associated variants in FGF13 are thought to affect NaV function, this has not been demonstrated in neurons and the contribution of other FGF13 functions has not been investigated, thus preventing an understanding of disease pathology and the development of precision therapies.
evidence: This is a statement about gaps in the existing literature that the current study addresses.

claim: DEE associated variants in FGF13 have been proposed to cause gain-of-function effects in excitatory neurons.
source: Lack of mechanistic clarity also arises because DEE associated variants in FGF13 have been proposed to cause gain-of-function effects in excitatory neurons (Fry et al., 2021) or via an apparently contradictory loss-of-function mechanism in inhibitory neurons (Puranam et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Fry et al., 2021).

claim: DEE associated variants in FGF13 have been proposed to cause loss-of-function effects in inhibitory neurons.
source: Lack of mechanistic clarity also arises because DEE associated variants in FGF13 have been proposed to cause gain-of-function effects in excitatory neurons (Fry et al., 2021) or via an apparently contradictory loss-of-function mechanism in inhibitory neurons (Puranam et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Puranam et al., 2015).

claim: FGF13 can generate multiple isoforms driven by alternative promoter usage and consequent alternative splicing.
source: Further complicating mechanistic understanding, FGF13 can generate multiple isoforms, driven by alternative promoter usage and consequent alternative splicing, with different but overlapping functions (Munoz-Sanjuan et al., 2000; Puranam et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Munoz-Sanjuan et al., 2000; Puranam et al., 2015).

claim: Alternatively spliced Fgf13 mRNAs exhibit distinct cell type-specific expression in the mouse cortex.
source: We recently discovered that alternatively spliced Fgf13 mRNAs exhibit distinct cell type-specific expression in the mouse cortex.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' prior work (Joglekar et al., 2021).

claim: In the developing mouse brain excitatory neurons express almost exclusively Fgf13-S.
source: In the developing mouse brain excitatory neurons express almost exclusively Fgf13-S while inhibitory neurons express both Fgf13-S and Fgf13-VY, a notable example of differential expression of an alternatively spliced neuronal gene in excitatory vs. inhibitory neurons (Furlanis et al., 2019; Joglekar et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Furlanis et al., 2019; Joglekar et al., 2021).

claim: In the developing mouse brain inhibitory neurons express both Fgf13-S and Fgf13-VY.
source: In the developing mouse brain excitatory neurons express almost exclusively Fgf13-S while inhibitory neurons express both Fgf13-S and Fgf13-VY, a notable example of differential expression of an alternatively spliced neuronal gene in excitatory vs. inhibitory neurons (Furlanis et al., 2019; Joglekar et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Furlanis et al., 2019; Joglekar et al., 2021).

claim: DEE-associated variants in FGF13 have been identified in FGF13-S and modeled as causing pro-excitatory NaV channel dysfunction in excitatory neurons.
source: DEE-associated variants in FGF13 have been identified in FGF13-S and modeled as causing pro-excitatory NaV channel dysfunction in excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about prior work in the field that the authors are building upon.

claim: A maternally transmitted chromosomal translocation that disrupts the X-linked FGF13 locus and eliminates FGF13-VY expression while preserving expression of FGF13-S causes a seizure disorder in two brothers.
source: Conversely, a maternally transmitted chromosomal translocation that disrupts the X-linked FGF13 locus and eliminates FGF13-VY expression while preserving expression of FGF13-S causes a seizure disorder in two brothers (Puranam et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Puranam et al., 2015).

claim: Nestin-Fgf13 cKO male mice showed near complete absence of FGF13 in hippocampi by western blot.
source: In hippocampi from Nestin-Fgf13 cKO brains we observed near complete absence of FGF13 (Figure 1B) by western blot and by immunohistochemistry (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Nestin-Fgf13 cKO male mice showed near complete absence of FGF13 in hippocampi by immunohistochemistry.
source: In hippocampi from Nestin-Fgf13 cKO brains we observed near complete absence of FGF13 (Figure 1B) by western blot and by immunohistochemistry (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In WT mice, FGF13 signal is prominent in the hippocampal pyramidal cell layer as well as in sparse presumed interneuron somata throughout all layers.
source: In WT mice, FGF13 signal is prominent in the hippocampal pyramidal cell layer as well as in sparse presumed interneuron somata (see below) throughout all layers.
evidence: This is an observation from immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Offspring from Nestin-Fgf13 crosses were born at expected Mendelian ratios.
source: Offspring were born at expected Mendelian ratios (Table 1), but all Nestin-Fgf13 cKO male mice died before weaning with a median survival age of 17 days postnatal (P17; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 1.

claim: All Nestin-Fgf13 cKO male mice died before weaning with a median survival age of 17 days postnatal (P17).
source: Offspring were born at expected Mendelian ratios (Table 1), but all Nestin-Fgf13 cKO male mice died before weaning with a median survival age of 17 days postnatal (P17; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Nestin-Fgf13 Het females exhibited postnatal death, with only 60% surviving past 1 month.
source: Nestin-Fgf13 Het females also exhibited postnatal death, with only 60% surviving past 1 month (Figure 1D), implying a gene dosage effect of Fgf13 loss.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The reduced survival of Nestin-Fgf13 Het females implies a gene dosage effect of Fgf13 loss.
source: Nestin-Fgf13 Het females also exhibited postnatal death, with only 60% surviving past 1 month (Figure 1D), implying a gene dosage effect of Fgf13 loss.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the survival data comparing hemizygous males and heterozygous females.

claim: Nestin-Fgf13 cKO male mice suffered spontaneous seizures in their home cage as early as P12.
source: Nestin-Fgf13 cKO male mice suffered spontaneous seizures in their home cage (Video 1) as early as P12, followed by premature death (Figure 1D), consistent with mouse models of DEE that exhibit SUDEP (Bunton-Stasyshyn et al., 2019; Han et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by video evidence (Video 1) and survival data (Figure 1D).

claim: Nestin-Fgf13 cKO males were smaller than their wild type littermates by P14.
source: Nestin-Fgf13 cKO males were smaller than their wild type littermates by P14 (Figure 1E), suggesting developmental delay, likely a consequence of recurrent seizures and consistent with DEE mouse models (Yu et al., 2006; Kalume et al., 2013; Teran et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by body mass data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The smaller size of Nestin-Fgf13 cKO males suggests developmental delay, likely a consequence of recurrent seizures.
source: Nestin-Fgf13 cKO males were smaller than their wild type littermates by P14 (Figure 1E), suggesting developmental delay, likely a consequence of recurrent seizures and consistent with DEE mouse models (Yu et al., 2006; Kalume et al., 2013; Teran et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed phenotype and comparison to other DEE models cited.

claim: All Nestin-Fgf13 cKO mice exhibited tonic-clonic seizures during the hyperthermic seizure protocol while wild type mice remained seizure free.
source: All Nestin-Fgf13 cKO males exhibited tonic-clonic seizures during the hyperthermic seizure protocol while wild type mice remained seizure free (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In Emx1-Fgf13 cKO mice, western blots showed the loss of two FGF13 isoforms (FGF13-S and FGF13-U).
source: In Emx1-Fgf13 cKO mice, western blots showed the loss of two FGF13 isoforms (Figure 2A), FGF13-S and FGF13-U, consistent with single-cell long-read RNA sequencing that showed that excitatory neurons predominantly express FGF13-S (Joglekar et al., 2021), which we confirmed with a FGF13-S specific antibody (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Excitatory neurons predominantly express FGF13-S.
source: In Emx1-Fgf13 cKO mice, western blots showed the loss of two FGF13 isoforms (Figure 2A), FGF13-S and FGF13-U, consistent with single-cell long-read RNA sequencing that showed that excitatory neurons predominantly express FGF13-S (Joglekar et al., 2021), which we confirmed with a FGF13-S specific antibody (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by prior single-cell RNA sequencing data (Joglekar et al., 2021) and confirmed by western blot with a FGF13-S specific antibody.

claim: FGF13-VY and FGF13-V are the major isoforms expressed in inhibitory interneurons.
source: FGF13-VY and FGF13-V, the major isoforms expressed in inhibitory interneurons (Joglekar et al., 2021), were preserved.
evidence: This is supported by prior single-cell RNA sequencing data (Joglekar et al., 2021).

claim: Fluorescent immunohistochemistry of hippocampi from Emx1-Fgf13 cKO showed loss of FGF13 from the CA1 pyramidal cell layer but maintenance of FGF13 signal from sparse putative interneuron somata.
source: Fluorescent immunohistochemistry of hippocampi from Emx1-Fgf13 cKO showed loss of FGF13 from the CA1 pyramidal cell layer but maintenance of FGF13 signal from sparse putative interneuron somata (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Emx1-Fgf13 cKO mice were born at expected Mendelian ratios.
source: Emx1-Fgf13 cKO mice were born at expected Mendelian ratios (Table 1) and all survived to adulthood (Figure 2C), similar to a previous report (Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 1.

claim: All Emx1-Fgf13 cKO mice survived to adulthood.
source: Emx1-Fgf13 cKO mice were born at expected Mendelian ratios (Table 1) and all survived to adulthood (Figure 2C), similar to a previous report (Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2C and is consistent with a prior report (Wu et al., 2012).

claim: Average body size and mass at P14 revealed no differences between wild type and Emx1-Fgf13 cKO genotypes.
source: Average body size and mass at P14 revealed no differences between wild type and Emx1-Fgf13 cKO genotypes (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by body mass data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: None of the Emx1-Fgf13 cKO succumbed to seizures during the hyperthermia protocol.
source: None of the Emx1-Fgf13 cKO succumbed to seizures during the hyperthermia protocol (Figure 2E), and EEG recordings during the hyperthermia protocol confirmed no seizure activity in Emx1-Fgf13 cKO or wild type mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: EEG recordings during the hyperthermia protocol confirmed no seizure activity in Emx1-Fgf13 cKO or wild type mice.
source: None of the Emx1-Fgf13 cKO succumbed to seizures during the hyperthermia protocol (Figure 2E), and EEG recordings during the hyperthermia protocol confirmed no seizure activity in Emx1-Fgf13 cKO or wild type mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by EEG data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Loss of Fgf13 from excitatory forebrain neurons is not sufficient to induce seizure susceptibility.
source: These data show that loss of Fgf13 from excitatory forebrain neurons is not sufficient to induce seizure susceptibility.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing no seizures in Emx1-Fgf13 cKO mice.

claim: Emx1-Fgf13 cKO neurons exhibit diminished long-term inactivation.
source: To assess for long-term inactivation, we applied successive depolarizations (Figure 2G) and observed successive reductions in peak current in WT neurons, a process blunted in Emx1-Fgf13 cKO neurons.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Fgf13 ablation in Emx1+ neurons diminished long-term inactivation, but this deficit is not sufficient to cause seizures.
source: Thus, although Fgf13 ablation in Emx1+ neurons diminished long-term inactivation—similar to that observed for DEE associated variants in FGF13-S expressed in Neuro2A cells (Fry et al., 2021)—these data suggest that FGF13-S dysfunction in excitatory neurons is an unlikely contributor to a pro-excitatory state and seizures.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing diminished long-term inactivation but no seizures in Emx1-Fgf13 cKO mice.

claim: One-third of the GFP+ interneurons expressed FGF13 at P13.
source: With immunohistochemistry on brains from mice in which a Gad2-Cre driver (Taniguchi et al., 2011) expressed a Cre-dependent GFP (Ai6) reporter (Madisen et al., 2010) in inhibitory interneurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B), one-third of the GFP+ interneurons expressed FGF13 at P13 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The FGF13 signal by immunohistochemistry was completely eliminated from the GFP+ cells in mouse brains expressing GFP from the Gad2-Cre driver in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice.
source: The FGF13 signal by immunohistochemistry was completely eliminated from the GFP+ cells in mouse brains also expressing GFP from the Gad2-Cre driver while the diffuse staining pattern in the excitatory pyramidal cell layer and overall hippocampal morphology were unaffected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B.

evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice, the most significant reduction was in FGF13-VY and FGF13-Y while FGF13-S was partially spared.

evidence: This is supported by western blot data and is consistent with prior transcript analysis (Joglekar et al., 2021).

claim: None of the male Gad2-Fgf13 cKO hemizygous knockout mice survived to adulthood.

claim: The median survival in male Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice was 14.5 days.

claim: Survivors at P14 in male Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice were smaller than their wild type littermates.

claim: The survival deficit in female Gad2-Fgf13 Het mice suggests a gene dosage effect.

claim: Brains of male Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice were smaller compared to wild type littermates.
source: Brains of male Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice were smaller compared to wild type littermates, as was body size (Figure 3E).

claim: All Gad2-Fgf13 cKO males suffered tonic-clonic seizures during the hyperthermia-induced seizure protocol while wild type littermates did not.

evidence: This is an observation from the experimental protocol.

claim: The unwitnessed premature deaths in the home cage were likely related to recurrent seizures.
source: With witnessed seizures immediately preceding death in some mice, we interpret that the previously noted unwitnessed premature deaths in the home cage were likely related to recurrent seizures.
evidence: This is an inference based on observed seizures preceding death.

claim: FGF13 deficiency in inhibitory cells is the major contributor to the seizures and premature mortality seen in the Nestin-Fgf13 cKO mice.
source: Together, these data suggest that FGF13 deficiency in inhibitory cells, rather than excitatory cells, is the major contributor to the seizures and premature mortality seen in the Nestin-Fgf13 cKO mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing phenotypes across different knockout models.

claim: Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice did not have a deficit of interneurons underlying their seizure phenotype.
source: We found no difference in the number of Gad2-GFP+hippocampal neurons between genotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), indicating that Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice did not have a deficit of interneurons underlying their seizure phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of Gad2-GFP+ neurons shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: An unbiased metabolomic analysis on brains from Gad2-Fgf13 cKO and WT control mice revealed marked differences between genotypes.
source: Further, an unbiased metabolomic analysis on brains from Gad2-Fgf13 cKO and WT control mice revealed marked differences between genotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary file 2) and several features consistent with severe seizures.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomic data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The metabolite most enriched in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO brains was L-kynurenine.
source: For example, the metabolite most enriched in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO brains was L-kynurenine (Log2fold change = 2.58, p=0.0009), a metabolite most enriched in patients with status epilepticus (Hanin et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomic data and comparison to patient data (Hanin et al., 2024).

claim: L-kynurenine is a metabolite most enriched in patients with status epilepticus.
source: For example, the metabolite most enriched in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO brains was L-kynurenine (Log2fold change = 2.58, p=0.0009), a metabolite most enriched in patients with status epilepticus (Hanin et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature (Hanin et al., 2024).

claim: The most enriched KEGG pathway among upregulated metabolites in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO vs. WT was glycolysis.
source: Metabolite set enrichment analysis in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO vs. WT revealed that the most enriched Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway among upregulated metabolites was glycolysis (p=4.29E-6), also consistent with data obtained in patients in status epilepticus (Hanin et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by metabolite set enrichment analysis and comparison to patient data (Hanin et al., 2024).

claim: The most downregulated pathway in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO vs. WT was methionine metabolism.
source: The most downregulated pathway was methionine metabolism (p=9.88E-4), consistent with methionine synthase deficiency—an inborn error of metabolism—that presents with seizures (Kripps et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by metabolite set enrichment analysis and comparison to a genetic disorder (Kripps et al., 2022).

claim: The metabolomic analysis supported the severity of the seizure phenotype observed in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice.

evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the metabolomic data.

claim: The highest enrichment of Fgf13 in CA1 interneurons was in subsets assigned as axo-axonic and medial ganglionic eminence (MGE) neurogliaform/Ivy cells.

claim: Fgf13 expression has been identified in Nkx2.1+ MGE-derived interneurons, including axo-axonic chandelier cells.
source: Further, Fgf13 expression has previously been identified in Nkx2.1+ MGE-derived interneurons, including axo-axonic chandelier cells (Paul et al., 2017; Mahadevan et al., 2021), which depend upon Fgf13 expression for proper development (Favuzzi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Paul et al., 2017; Mahadevan et al., 2021; Favuzzi et al., 2019).

claim: Chandelier cells depend upon Fgf13 expression for proper development.
source: Further, Fgf13 expression has previously been identified in Nkx2.1+ MGE-derived interneurons, including axo-axonic chandelier cells (Paul et al., 2017; Mahadevan et al., 2021), which depend upon Fgf13 expression for proper development (Favuzzi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature (Favuzzi et al., 2019).

claim: Single-cell profiling of human postmortem cortical tissue has identified high FGF13 expression in neurogliaform and parvalbumin interneurons throughout early development.
source: Single-cell profiling of human postmortem cortical tissue has identified high FGF13 expression in neurogliaform and parvalbumin interneurons throughout early development (Herring et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature (Herring et al., 2022).

claim: Nkx2.1-Fgf13 cKO mice were born at expected Mendelian ratios.
source: Nkx2.1-Fgf13 cKO mice were born at expected Mendelian ratios (Table 1) but only ~40% of male Nkx2.1-Fgf13 cKO mice survived past 1 month of age (Figure 3—figure supplement 4D), consistent with a partial loss of FGF13 expression in hippocampal interneurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).

claim: Only ~40% of male Nkx2.1-Fgf13 cKO mice survived past 1 month of age.
source: Nkx2.1-Fgf13 cKO mice were born at expected Mendelian ratios (Table 1) but only ~40% of male Nkx2.1-Fgf13 cKO mice survived past 1 month of age (Figure 3—figure supplement 4D), consistent with a partial loss of FGF13 expression in hippocampal interneurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4D.

claim: The median survival age for male Nkx2.1-Fgf13 cKO mice was 22 days (P22).
source: The median survival age for male Nkx2.1-Fgf13 cKO mice was 22 days (P22), and surviving mutants were smaller than their wild type littermates at P14 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: This is supported by survival data.

claim: Surviving male Nkx2.1-Fgf13 cKO mutants were smaller than their wild type littermates at P14.
source: The median survival age for male Nkx2.1-Fgf13 cKO mice was 22 days (P22), and surviving mutants were smaller than their wild type littermates at P14 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E).

claim: Female Nkx2.1-Fgf13 Het survived to adulthood.
source: Female Nkx2.1-Fgf13 Het survived to adulthood.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the survival data.

claim: Almost all male Nkx2.1-Fgf13 cKO suffered tonic-clonic seizures during the hyperthermia induction protocol, while wild type littermates did not.
source: We found that almost all male Nkx2.1-Fgf13 cKO suffered tonic-clonic seizures during the hyperthermia induction protocol, while wild type littermates did not (Figure 3—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4F.

claim: MGE-derived neurons are partially responsible for the phenotype observed in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice.
source: Because the lethality and seizure susceptibility in the Nkx2.1-Fgf13 cKO mice were reduced compared to the Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice, we hypothesize that MGE-derived neurons are partially responsible for the phenotype observed in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on comparing phenotypes between Nkx2.1-Fgf13 cKO and Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice.

claim: Pyramidal cells in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO hippocampi showed an increased frequency of sEPSCs compared to wild type littermates.
source: Pyramidal cells in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO hippocampi, compared to wild type littermates, showed an increased frequency of sEPSCs (Figure 4A–B) and a decreased frequency of sIPSCs mice relative to wild type littermates (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4A–B.

claim: Pyramidal cells in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO hippocampi showed a decreased frequency of sIPSCs compared to wild type littermates.
source: Pyramidal cells in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO hippocampi, compared to wild type littermates, showed an increased frequency of sEPSCs (Figure 4A–B) and a decreased frequency of sIPSCs mice relative to wild type littermates (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4C–D.

claim: There was no significant change in sEPSC or sIPSC amplitude in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO pyramidal cells.
source: Because there was no significant change in sEPSC or sIPSC amplitude (Figure 4B and D), the increased sEPSC and decreased sIPSC frequencies indicate a presynaptic and not postsynaptic mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4B and D.

claim: The increased sEPSC and decreased sIPSC frequencies indicate a presynaptic and not postsynaptic mechanism.
source: Because there was no significant change in sEPSC or sIPSC amplitude (Figure 4B and D), the increased sEPSC and decreased sIPSC frequencies indicate a presynaptic and not postsynaptic mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological data showing changes in frequency but not amplitude.

claim: Ablation of Fgf13 specifically in inhibitory neurons decreased direct and downstream inhibitory drive onto pyramidal cells, thereby increasing pyramidal cell excitability.
source: Together, these data suggest that ablation of Fgf13 specifically in inhibitory neurons (in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice) decreased direct and downstream inhibitory drive onto pyramidal cells, thereby increasing pyramidal cell excitability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiological data showing increased sEPSC and decreased sIPSC frequencies.

claim: At low levels (<100 pA) current injection elicited a similar number of spikes in neurons from Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice compared to WT.
source: At low levels (<100 pA) current injection elicited a similar number of spikes in neurons from Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice (albeit spike morphology and frequency were different, see below) but the number of spikes then plateaued and was less than the number elicited in neurons from WT mice at higher amounts of current injection (Figure 5B), suggesting a decrease in intrinsic excitability in neurons from Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: At higher amounts of current injection, the number of spikes in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO neurons plateaued and was less than the number elicited in neurons from WT mice.
source: At low levels (<100 pA) current injection elicited a similar number of spikes in neurons from Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice (albeit spike morphology and frequency were different, see below) but the number of spikes then plateaued and was less than the number elicited in neurons from WT mice at higher amounts of current injection (Figure 5B), suggesting a decrease in intrinsic excitability in neurons from Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The reduced number of spikes at higher current injection suggests a decrease in intrinsic excitability in neurons from Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice.
source: At low levels (<100 pA) current injection elicited a similar number of spikes in neurons from Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice (albeit spike morphology and frequency were different, see below) but the number of spikes then plateaued and was less than the number elicited in neurons from WT mice at higher amounts of current injection (Figure 5B), suggesting a decrease in intrinsic excitability in neurons from Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological data.

claim: More Gad2-Fgf13 cKO cells entered depolarization block, and at lower levels of current injection than wildtype interneurons.
source: Examination of individual traces revealed that more Gad2-Fgf13 cKO cells entered depolarization block, and at lower levels of current injection than wildtype interneurons (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Resting membrane potential, rheobase, and threshold potential were not different between Gad2-Fgf13 cKO and WT genotypes.
source: Resting membrane potential, rheobase, and threshold potential were not different between genotypes, Figure 5D.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In Gad2-Fgf13 cKO interneurons there was a progressive reduction in the action potential peak amplitude and dV/dt max in the second and third elicited action potentials.

Most notably, in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO interneurons we observed a progressive reduction in the action potential peak amplitude and dV/dt max, an increase in APD50, and a greater increase in the interspike membrane voltage (Figure 5F–G), suggesting a growing repolarization deficit in the Gad2-Fgf13 cKO neurons each subsequent spike, thus increasing the likelihood to undergo depolarization block.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5F–G.

claim: In Gad2-Fgf13 cKO interneurons there was an increase in APD50 in the second and third elicited action potentials.
source: However, we observed marked genotype differences in the second and third elicited action potentials. Most notably, in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO interneurons we observed a progressive reduction in the action potential peak amplitude and dV/dt max, an increase in APD50, and a greater increase in the interspike membrane voltage (Figure 5F–G), suggesting a growing repolarization deficit in the Gad2-Fgf13 cKO neurons each subsequent spike, thus increasing the likelihood to undergo depolarization block.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5F–G.

evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5F–G.

evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological data.

claim: No differences in NaV current amplitude were observed between Gad2-Fgf13 cKO neurons and wild type controls.
source: Indeed, we observed no differences in current amplitude nor steady-state inactivation between Gad2-Fgf13 cKO neurons and wild type controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No differences in steady-state inactivation were observed between Gad2-Fgf13 cKO neurons and wild type controls.
source: Indeed, we observed no differences in current amplitude nor steady-state inactivation between Gad2-Fgf13 cKO neurons and wild type controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A reduced Kv current density was observed in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO interneurons compared to WT neurons.
source: Since in cardiomyocytes we showed that FGF13 can also affect various KV channels that contribute to the repolarizing phase of the cardiac action potential (Wang et al., 2017), here we recorded macroscopic potassium currents and observed a reduced Kv current density in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO interneurons compared to WT neurons (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: After viral re-expression of Fgf13-VY or Fgf13-S, neither threshold potential nor rheobase were affected and were not different compared to values from either WT or Gad2-Fgf13 cKO neurons.
source: After viral re-expression of Fgf13-VY or Fgf13-S, neither threshold potential nor rheobase were affected and were not different compared to values from either WT or Gad2-Fgf13 cKO neurons (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: After rescue with either Fgf13-VY or Fgf13-S, current injection >100 pA elicited more action potentials than in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO neurons, suggesting that excitability was at least partially restored.
source: After rescue with either Fgf13-VY or Fgf13-S, current injection >100 pA elicited more action potentials than in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO neurons, suggesting that excitability was at least partially restored (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Compared to Gad2-Fgf13 cKO neurons a smaller fraction of Gad2+ cells re-expressing Fgf13-VY or Fgf13-S reached depolarization block when injected with >100 pA.
source: Indeed, compared to Gad2-Fgf13 cKO neurons a smaller fraction of Gad2+ cells re-expressing Fgf13-VY or Fgf13-S reached depolarization block when injected with >100 pA (Figure 6D), although neither Fgf13-VY nor Fgf13-S alone reduced the probability of conduction block to what was observed in WT neurons.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Neither Fgf13-VY nor Fgf13-S alone reduced the probability of conduction block to what was observed in WT neurons.
source: Indeed, compared to Gad2-Fgf13 cKO neurons a smaller fraction of Gad2+ cells re-expressing Fgf13-VY or Fgf13-S reached depolarization block when injected with >100 pA (Figure 6D), although neither Fgf13-VY nor Fgf13-S alone reduced the probability of conduction block to what was observed in WT neurons.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data showing partial rescue.

claim: Neither Fgf13-S nor Fgf13-VY rescue was able to prevent the prolongation of APD50 observed in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO neurons.
source: Examination of specific parameters revealed that neither Fgf13-S nor Fgf13-VY rescue was able to prevent the prolongation of APD50 nor reduction in the action potential amplitude, dV/dt max or action potential peak amplitude observed in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO neurons (Figure 6F), again suggesting that neither FGF13-S nor FGF13-VY is sufficient for maintaining excitability in Gad2 neurons.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Infection with Fgf13-S partially hyperpolarized the interspike membrane potential compared to Gad2-Fgf13 cKO.
source: On the other hand, infection with Fgf13-S partially hyperpolarized the interspike membrane potential (compared to Gad2-Fgf13 cKO, Figure 6G), suggesting that FGF13-S increased the repolarizing K+ currents.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: FGF13-S increased the repolarizing K+ currents.
source: On the other hand, infection with Fgf13-S partially hyperpolarized the interspike membrane potential (compared to Gad2-Fgf13 cKO, Figure 6G), suggesting that FGF13-S increased the repolarizing K+ currents.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed hyperpolarization of the interspike membrane potential.

claim: Infection with Fgf13-S but not Fgf13-VY increased K+ current density to WT levels.
source: Indeed, infection with Fgf13-S but not Fgf13-VY increased K+ current density to WT levels (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: FGF13-S and FGF13-VY, both expressed in inhibitory interneurons, contribute to inhibitory interneuron function and modulation of pyramidal neuron excitability.
source: These data suggest that FGF13-S and FGF13-VY, both expressed in inhibitory interneurons (Joglekar et al., 2021) contribute to inhibitory interneuron function and modulation of pyramidal neuron excitability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments and prior expression data.

claim: Fgf13 ablation and consequent loss of FGF13-S and FGF13-VY in a subset of interneurons reduced overall inhibitory drive from Fgf13-expressing interneurons onto hippocampal pyramidal neurons.
source: We found that Fgf13 ablation and consequent loss of FGF13-S and FGF13-VY in a subset of interneurons reduced overall inhibitory drive from Fgf13-expressing interneurons onto hippocampal pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the electrophysiological experiments.

claim: Both FGF13-S and FGF13-VY isoforms are required for proper interneuron function as re-expression of FGF13-S or FGF13-VY only partially restored excitability.
source: Rescue experiments suggest that both FGF13-S and FGF13-VY isoforms are required for proper interneuron function as re-expression of FGF13-S or FGF13-VY only partially restored excitability (our experimental setup did not allow rescue with both isoforms simultaneously).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments.

claim: The data resolve apparently conflicting reports in which reduced inhibitory interneuron function contrasts with a model that proposes that FGF13 variants within excitatory neurons drive increased excitability.
source: Building upon our recent analysis of Fgf13 splice variant expression (Joglekar et al., 2021), our data resolve apparently conflicting reports in which reduced inhibitory interneuron function, suggested as the main contributor in a global Fgf13 female heterozygous knockout model, (Puranam et al., 2015) contrasts with a model that proposes that FGF13 variants within excitatory neurons drive increased excitability because of diminished long-term inactivation (Fry et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study's findings in the context of prior literature.

claim: Alternative splicing is an important source of protein diversity in the mammalian brain.
source: The apparent requirement of both FGF13-S and FGF13-VY extends previous studies showing their distinct roles in neurons (Pablo et al., 2016) and emphasizes that alternative splicing is an important source of protein diversity in the mammalian brain, an evolutionarily conserved feature thought to contribute to the nervous system's complexity (Raj and Blencowe, 2015; Zhang et al., 2016; Karlsson and Linnarsson, 2017; Porter et al., 2018; Furlanis et al., 2019; Joglekar et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Raj and Blencowe, 2015; Zhang et al., 2016; Karlsson and Linnarsson, 2017; Porter et al., 2018; Furlanis et al., 2019; Joglekar et al., 2023).

claim: Cell-specific alternative splicing in the brain has been posited as a mechanism to efficiently adapt to the external environment by quickly modifying protein activity.
source: Cell-specific alternative splicing in the brain has been posited as a mechanism to efficiently adapt to the external environment by quickly modifying protein activity (Lipscombe and Lopez Soto, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature (Lipscombe and Lopez Soto, 2019).

claim: FGF13 has the most extensive set of alternatively spliced isoforms among FHFs.
source: Not only does FGF13 have the most extensive set of alternatively spliced isoforms among FHFs (Smallwood et al., 1996; Munoz-Sanjuan et al., 2000; Pablo et al., 2016), but long-range single-cell sequencing data show that Fgf13 has a uniquely (among FHFs) segregated alternative splice variant expression pattern among distinct neuron cell type.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Smallwood et al., 1996; Munoz-Sanjuan et al., 2000; Pablo et al., 2016).

claim: Fgf13 has a uniquely segregated alternative splice variant expression pattern among distinct neuron cell types.
source: Not only does FGF13 have the most extensive set of alternatively spliced isoforms among FHFs (Smallwood et al., 1996; Munoz-Sanjuan et al., 2000; Pablo et al., 2016), but long-range single-cell sequencing data show that Fgf13 has a uniquely (among FHFs) segregated alternative splice variant expression pattern among distinct neuron cell type.
evidence: This is supported by long-range single-cell sequencing data.

claim: Among all genes, Fgf13 has one of the highest differential isoform expression (DIE) values across multiple neuronal cell-types.
source: Further, among all genes, Fgf13 has one of the highest differential isoform expression (DIE) values across multiple neuronal cell-types (Joglekar et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature (Joglekar et al., 2021).

claim: The current results are consistent with the available patient data.
source: Our results are also consistent with the available patient data.
evidence: This is a statement about the consistency of the current findings with prior patient data.

claim: The current data provide a unifying explanation for reports of FGF13 variants causing DEEs through different mechanisms.
source: As our data suggest that both FGF13-S and FGF13-VY contribute within inhibitory interneurons, we provide a unifying explanation for those reports.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study's findings.

claim: The inability to rescue electrophysiological consequences completely with either FGF13-S or FGF13-VY alone leaves open the possibility that other isoforms also make critical contributions.
source: Here, we were able to assess FGF13-S and FGF13-VY, chosen because they are most abundantly expressed isoforms in the adult mouse brain, but the inability to rescue electrophysiological consequences completely with either isoform alone leaves open the possibility that other isoforms (e.g. FGF13-U, FGF13-V) also make critical contributions.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the incomplete rescue observed in the experiments.

claim: Fgf13 silencing in Nkx2.1-CreER targeted neurons reduced the number of chandelier cell boutons.
source: Fgf13 silencing in Nkx2.1-CreER targeted neurons reduced the number of chandelier cell boutons (Favuzzi et al., 2019) and a more general role for FGF13 in interneuron development was suggested by a human scRNA-seq dataset (Herring et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature (Favuzzi et al., 2019).

claim: A more general role for FGF13 in interneuron development was suggested by a human scRNA-seq dataset.
source: Fgf13 silencing in Nkx2.1-CreER targeted neurons reduced the number of chandelier cell boutons (Favuzzi et al., 2019) and a more general role for FGF13 in interneuron development was suggested by a human scRNA-seq dataset (Herring et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature (Herring et al., 2022).

claim: Seizure susceptibility was attributable solely to Fgf13 knockout in inhibitory interneurons.
source: Our data here, in which seizure susceptibility was attributable solely to Fgf13 knockout in inhibitory interneurons and our demonstration that Fgf13 knockout restricted to Nkx2.1-expressing neurons increased seizure susceptibility—albeit to a lesser extent than complete knockout in inhibitory interneurons—support not only a possible role for Fgf13 in chandelier cell development but also confirm more general inhibitory interneuron roles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing different knockout models.

claim: The reduced survival of female heterozygote knockout animals implies a gene dosage effect within interneurons.
source: Along with the reduced seizure susceptibility of female heterozygote knockout animals, these data also imply a gene dosage effect within interneurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing phenotypes between hemizygous males and heterozygous females.

claim: The differences in survival among Gad2-Fgf13 cKO, Gad2-Fgf13 Het, Nkx2.1-Fgf13 cKO, and Nkx2.1-Fgf13 Het suggest a gene-dosage effect.
source: The differences in survival among Gad2-Fgf13 cKO, Gad2-Fgf13 Het, Nkx2.1-Fgf13 cKO, and Nkx2.1-Fgf13 Het also suggest a gene-dosage effect.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing survival data across different genotypes.

claim: Recurrent uncontrolled seizures are a major risk factor for sudden death.
source: We also observed occasional seizures in the home cage for all genotypes in which Fgf13 was ablated in interneurons (Nestin-Fgf13 cKO, Nkx2.1-Fgf13 cKO, and Gad2-Fgf13 cKO) and often discovered dead mice, which we suspect was a SUDEP phenotype due to recurrent seizures, given that recurrent uncontrolled seizures are a major risk factor for sudden death (Devinsky et al., 2016; Richerson, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Devinsky et al., 2016; Richerson, 2023).

claim: The data provide a clear connection between ablation of Fgf13 in inhibitory neurons and seizure susceptibility.
source: While our data provide a clear connection between ablation of Fgf13 in inhibitory neurons and seizure susceptibility, we find that Fgf13 ablation in excitatory neurons does not increase seizure susceptibility.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Fgf13 ablation in excitatory neurons does not increase seizure susceptibility.
source: While our data provide a clear connection between ablation of Fgf13 in inhibitory neurons and seizure susceptibility, we find that Fgf13 ablation in excitatory neurons does not increase seizure susceptibility.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Emx1-Fgf13 cKO mice.

claim: Complete neuronal knockout with Nestin-Cre conferred a relative increased survival compared to the interneuron-specific knockout with Gad2-Cre.
source: Indeed, complete neuronal knockout with Nestin-Cre conferred a relative increased survival compared to the interneuron-specific knockout with Gad2-Cre.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing survival data between different knockout models.

claim: The relative increased survival in the Nestin-Fgf13 cKO mice could be due to less efficient targeting of interneurons by Nestin-Cre.
source: We speculate that this relative increased survival in the Nestin-Fgf13 cKO mice could be technical, due to less efficient targeting of interneurons by Nestin-Cre (Liang et al., 2012), but it may also be biological if Nestin-Cre targeting of both excitatory and inhibitory neurons is comparatively neuroprotective because of simultaneous loss of both excitation and inhibition and consequent compensation for the loss of inhibition.
evidence: This is a speculation supported by a citation to prior literature (Liang et al., 2012).

claim: The relative increased survival in the Nestin-Fgf13 cKO mice may be biological if Nestin-Cre targeting of both excitatory and inhibitory neurons is comparatively neuroprotective because of simultaneous loss of both excitation and inhibition.
source: We speculate that this relative increased survival in the Nestin-Fgf13 cKO mice could be technical, due to less efficient targeting of interneurons by Nestin-Cre (Liang et al., 2012), but it may also be biological if Nestin-Cre targeting of both excitatory and inhibitory neurons is comparatively neuroprotective because of simultaneous loss of both excitation and inhibition and consequent compensation for the loss of inhibition.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed phenotypes.

claim: A global Fgf13 heterozygous mouse line survived with a normal life span.
source: The previous observation that a global Fgf13 heterozygous mouse line survived with a normal life span (Puranam et al., 2015) could support the interpretation that deletion from other cell types is comparatively neuroprotective.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature (Puranam et al., 2015).

claim: Emx1-Fgf13 cKO mice do not suffer seizures, consistent with an earlier study.
source: Moreover, our observations that our Emx1-Fgf13 cKO mice do not suffer seizures is consistent with an earlier study of Emx1-Fgf13 cKO mice, in which seizures were not reported (Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the current data and a citation to prior literature (Wu et al., 2012).

claim: FGF13-S confers long-term inactivation.
source: Previous studies suggested that FGF13-S, the isoform most highly expressed in excitatory neurons, confers long-term inactivation (Venkatesan et al., 2014; Fry et al., 2021), and the reduction of long-term inactivation due to DEE-associated variants drives increased excitability as the mechanism for seizures (Fry et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Venkatesan et al., 2014; Fry et al., 2021).

claim: The reduction of long-term inactivation due to DEE-associated variants drives increased excitability as the mechanism for seizures.
source: Previous studies suggested that FGF13-S, the isoform most highly expressed in excitatory neurons, confers long-term inactivation (Venkatesan et al., 2014; Fry et al., 2021), and the reduction of long-term inactivation due to DEE-associated variants drives increased excitability as the mechanism for seizures (Fry et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior literature (Fry et al., 2021) that the current study challenges.

claim: The current data confirm the ability of FGF13-S to impart long-term inactivation.
source: Our data confirm the ability of FGF13-S to impart long-term inactivation and that ablation of Fgf13 in excitatory neurons eliminates long-term inactivation, yet this mechanism does not likely contribute to seizure susceptibility.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data from Emx1-Fgf13 cKO neurons.

claim: Ablation of Fgf13 in excitatory neurons eliminates long-term inactivation, yet this mechanism does not likely contribute to seizure susceptibility.
source: Our data confirm the ability of FGF13-S to impart long-term inactivation and that ablation of Fgf13 in excitatory neurons eliminates long-term inactivation, yet this mechanism does not likely contribute to seizure susceptibility.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing loss of long-term inactivation but no seizures in Emx1-Fgf13 cKO mice.

claim: Knockout of Fgf13 in central nervous system excitatory neurons appears to affect learning and memory.
source: Rather, knockout of Fgf13 in central nervous system excitatory neurons appears to affect learning and memory (Wu et al., 2012), which we did not assess here.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature (Wu et al., 2012).

claim: The knockout models cannot provide direct insight into how missense variants reported in patients contribute to seizures.
source: An important limitation of our knockout models, however, is that they cannot provide direct insight into how missense variants reported in patients contribute to seizures.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current study.

claim: The Emx1-Fgf13 cKO model provides new boundaries on how missense variants act in excitatory neurons.
source: Nevertheless, since our Emx1-Fgf13 cKO mice show a loss of long-term inactivation in excitatory neurons—the proposed mechanism by which the missense variants drive seizures—our model provides new boundaries on how those missense variants act in excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Fgf13 ablation led to relatively minor effects on neuronal voltage-gated Na+ currents in Emx1+ excitatory neurons compared to previous results.
source: Further, other than long-term inactivation, data herein show that Fgf13 ablation led to relatively minor effects on neuronal voltage-gated Na+ currents in Emx1+ excitatory neurons compared to previous results from others and us (Venkatesan et al., 2014 Barbosa et al., 2017; Pablo et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2021; Shen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current data to prior literature (Venkatesan et al., 2014 Barbosa et al., 2017; Pablo et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2021; Shen et al., 2022).

claim: The knockout model represents a more relevant disease model than knockdown approaches or acute antibody infusion.
source: As the FGF13 DEEs result from a stable germ-line variants, the knockout model here (in contrast to knockdown approaches in cultured CNS neurons or acute infusion of antibodies) likely represents a more relevant disease model.
evidence: This is an inference about the relevance of the model system.

claim: Knockout of Fgf13 in Gad2+ neurons decreased excitability and reduced overall inhibitory drive to pyramidal cells, but surprisingly did not affect NaV currents in inhibitory neurons.
source: How does loss of FGF13 in inhibitory interneurons confer seizure susceptibility? Although knockout of Fgf13 in Gad2+ neurons decreased excitability and reduced overall inhibitory drive to pyramidal cells, knockout surprisingly did not affect NaV currents in inhibitory neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the electrophysiological experiments.

claim: The cytoplasmic C-terminal in NaV1.1 has a substitution of an amino acid that reduces FHF binding.
source: This conclusion fits well with our previous report that the cytoplasmic C-terminal in NaV1.1, the major NaV channel expressed in inhibitory neurons, has a substitution of an amino acid that reduces FHF binding (Wang et al., 2012), thus rendering these NaV1.1 channels—and thus NaV current in inhibitory interneurons—poor targets for FHF regulation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors (Wang et al., 2012).

claim: NaV1.1 channels are poor targets for FHF regulation.
source: This conclusion fits well with our previous report that the cytoplasmic C-terminal in NaV1.1, the major NaV channel expressed in inhibitory neurons, has a substitution of an amino acid that reduces FHF binding (Wang et al., 2012), thus rendering these NaV1.1 channels—and thus NaV current in inhibitory interneurons—poor targets for FHF regulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior work showing reduced FHF binding to NaV1.1.

claim: Perturbed excitability in interneurons lacking Fgf13 results from reduced K+ currents.
source: Rather, we found that perturbed excitability in interneurons lacking Fgf13 results from reduced K+ currents.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data showing reduced K+ current density in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO interneurons.

claim: Loss of FGF13 in cardiomyocytes reduces repolarizing KV currents.
source: This fits with our demonstration in cardiomyocytes that loss of FGF13 similarly reduces repolarizing KV currents (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors (Wang et al., 2017).

claim: FHFs exert effects beyond NaV channel regulation.
source: Moreover, these data build upon the growing recognition that FHFs exert effects beyond NaV channel regulation—the focus of most FHF studies since FHFs were identified as capable of directly interacting with NaV channel C-termini (Liu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current data and supported by a citation (Liu et al., 2001).

claim: The mechanism(s) by which FGF13 affects KV currents is not known.
source: The mechanism(s) by which FGF13 affects KV currents is not known—we have not detected direct interaction between FHFs and KV channels—but we speculate that the identified role for FGF13 in stabilizing microtubules may contribute, as microtubules regulate trafficking of ion channels to the plasma membrane during channel biogenesis (Vacher et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: The identified role for FGF13 in stabilizing microtubules may contribute to its effects on KV currents, as microtubules regulate trafficking of ion channels to the plasma membrane during channel biogenesis.
source: The mechanism(s) by which FGF13 affects KV currents is not known—we have not detected direct interaction between FHFs and KV channels—but we speculate that the identified role for FGF13 in stabilizing microtubules may contribute, as microtubules regulate trafficking of ion channels to the plasma membrane during channel biogenesis (Vacher et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by a citation to prior literature (Vacher et al., 2008).

claim: The data are consistent with a possible role for FGF13 in chandelier cell function.
source: Although we did not test it directly, our data are consistent with a possible role for FGF13 in chandelier cell function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and prior knowledge about chandelier cells.

claim: Chandelier cells are fast-spiking GABAergic interneurons that uniquely target the axon initial segment of pyramidal cells.
source: Chandelier cells are fast-spiking GABAergic interneurons that uniquely target the axon initial segment of pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about chandelier cells based on established knowledge.

claim: Chandelier cells are found sparsely in the brain, but are highly branched, enabling contact on hundreds of neighboring pyramidal cells.
source: Chandelier cells are found sparsely in the brain, but are highly branched, enabling contact on hundreds of neighboring pyramidal cells (Compans and Burrone, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature (Compans and Burrone, 2023).

claim: Fgf13 has been identified as a key molecule in the development of chandelier cell axons.
source: Fgf13 has previously been identified as a key molecule in the development of chandelier cell axons (Favuzzi et al., 2019), but whether Fgf13 subsequently contributes to their function has not been reported.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature (Favuzzi et al., 2019).

claim: Chandelier cells originate from the MGE, alongside parvalbumin- and somatostatin-expressing interneurons.
source: Chandelier cells originate from the MGE, alongside parvalbumin- and somatostatin-expressing interneurons (Gallo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature (Gallo et al., 2020).

claim: The Nkx2.1-Fgf13 cKO mice target deletion of Fgf13 from chandelier cells, parvalbumin-expressing interneurons, and somatostatin-expressing interneurons.
source: As our Nkx2.1-Fgf13 cKO mice target deletion of Fgf13 from all the above subtypes, our data suggest that FGF13 may regulate chandelier cell function in seizure generation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Cre driver used and knowledge of MGE-derived interneuron subtypes.

claim: FGF13 may regulate chandelier cell function in seizure generation.
source: As our Nkx2.1-Fgf13 cKO mice target deletion of Fgf13 from all the above subtypes, our data suggest that FGF13 may regulate chandelier cell function in seizure generation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental data.

claim: Chandelier cells have been shown to depolarize pyramidal cells and therefore exert a pro-excitatory role in the cortex.
source: Although chandelier cells have been shown to depolarize pyramidal cells and therefore exert a pro-excitatory role in the cortex (Szabadics et al., 2006), we observe otherwise in our mouse model in which decreased interneuron excitability results in a pro-excitatory state.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature (Szabadics et al., 2006).

claim: In the current mouse model, decreased interneuron excitability results in a pro-excitatory state.
source: Although chandelier cells have been shown to depolarize pyramidal cells and therefore exert a pro-excitatory role in the cortex (Szabadics et al., 2006), we observe otherwise in our mouse model in which decreased interneuron excitability results in a pro-excitatory state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.
